Lyle “Rusty” Dedrick was born in Delevan, New York on July 12, 1918. His family was engaged in farming but both he and his brother Art were attracted to the music business, taking up the trumpet and trombone. Starting in 1938, Rusty toured with Dick Stabile, Red Norvo and Claude Thornhill, eventually establishing himself in the active recording scene in New York City. He has arranged music for numerous ensembles and jazz artists and directed the Jazz Studies Department at the Manhattan School of Music in the 1970’s. His recordings include collaborations with Don Elliot and tributes to his favorite jazz soloists, including trumpeter Bunny Berigan.
Rusty was interviewed in Ellenville, New York on June 23, 1998, by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.
We are filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive in the Catskills, and it’s my pleasure to have trumpeter, arranger, composer and educator Lyle “Rusty” Dedrick. Thank you for coming.
You are an Upstate-New-York-raised, actually a long line of jazz musicians came from the Catskills.
When you were, let’s say ten, can you recall what the pop music of the day was like, and did it have an effect on you?

To some extent yes. Everyone in my family had, although I grew up on a farm, a little dairy farm outside of Buffalo, everyone in the family played an instrument. My father played the trombone, not the best but the loudest ever, you know in the country bands. I used to love to go and listen to the Saturday night concerts and stuff. That’s what kindled my earliest interest. And as far as the pop music, well I think we had a couple of sheets of music, my mother played piano and violin, my brother Art, who is better known, played the trombone way, way back, and I remember a song that we had a song copy of [sings] I’m a dreamer/Aren’t we all/Just a dreamer/Aren’t we all. And on and on. That would date us, that would pinpoint — and excuse my voice.
Well it’s curious because a lot of those tunes, maybe not that one, but some of those tunes became jazz standards later on.
I never knew why “Body and Soul” and not—
Well “Body and Soul” was not yet on the scene.
